title: Caves and Their Stone Icicles
summary: How slightly acidic rainwater carves limestone caves, how dripping water builds stalactites, stalagmites, and columns, and what Saudi Arabia's caves reveal about the past.
poll: Cave formations should be protected, even if it means fewer people can visit caves.

versions.title: Stone Icicles in Caves
versions.text:
Step in a cave. It is dark and cool. Shine a light up. Stone points hang down. They look like icicles. They are stalactites. Some grow up from the floor. They are stalagmites.

Most caves form in limestone rock. Rain picks up a gas. It comes from the air and dirt. The gas makes the rain a weak acid. The rain sinks in cracks in the rock. Bit by bit, it eats the rock. The cracks get wide. They turn to rooms and halls. It takes a long time.

It drips from the roof. Each drip holds a bit of rock. The drip lets the gas go. It leaves a thin ring of stone. Ring by ring, a stalactite grows down. Drops on the floor leave stone, too. A stalagmite grows up.

They grow so slow! In a hundred years, one may grow just a bit. When the two meet, they make a post. It is a column.

Saudi Arabia has caves, too. Lots are in a dry land. It is called the Summan. Their stone points grew long ago. There was more rain then.

Do not touch them. Oil from your hands can stop them. Then they can not grow.

versions.title: Caves and Stone Icicles
versions.text:
Step into a cave, and you will find that it is dark and cool. Shine a flashlight at the ceiling. You will see stone points hanging down like icicles. These are called stalactites. Other stone points rise up from the floor. These are called stalagmites.

Most caves form in a rock called limestone. As rain falls, it picks up a gas called carbon dioxide from the air and the soil. This gas turns the rain into a weak acid. The rain sinks into tiny cracks in the rock. Little by little, it dissolves the limestone. The cracks grow wider and wider until they become rooms and tunnels. This takes thousands and thousands of years.

Even after the cave forms, water keeps seeping in. It drips from the ceiling. Each drop carries a tiny bit of dissolved rock. As the drop hangs, it lets the gas escape. Then it leaves behind a thin ring of stone. Ring by ring, a stalactite grows down. Drops that land on the floor leave stone, too, so a stalagmite grows up.

These formations grow very slowly. In a hundred years, one may grow only about one centimeter. When a stalactite and a stalagmite finally meet, they join into a stone post called a column.

Saudi Arabia has caves, too. Many lie under a dry area called the Summan Plateau. Their stone points formed long ago, when Arabia got much more rain. Scientists study their layers to learn about rain in the past.

Please never touch these stones. The oil on your skin can stop them from growing.

versions.title: Caves and Their Stone Icicles
versions.text:
Step into a cave, and you will notice that it is dark, cool, and damp. Shine a flashlight at the ceiling, and you will see stone points hanging down like icicles. These are called stalactites. Similar points rise from the floor below them. These are called stalagmites.

Most caves form in a rock called limestone, which is made of a mineral called calcite. As rain falls, it picks up a gas called carbon dioxide from the air and the soil. This gas turns the rain into a weak acid. The water sinks into tiny cracks in the rock and slowly dissolves the limestone. Over thousands of years, the cracks grow wider until they become tunnels and huge rooms.

Even after the cave forms, water keeps seeping through the ceiling. Each drop carries a little dissolved calcite. As the drop hangs, it lets some of the gas escape. Then it leaves behind a thin ring of mineral. Ring by ring, a stalactite grows downward. Drops that fall to the floor leave calcite there, too, so a stalagmite grows upward.

Many people mix up the two names, so here is a trick. A stalactite has a c, for ceiling, and it hangs from the top. A stalagmite has a g, for ground, and it grows up from the floor.

These formations grow very slowly. In a hundred years, one may grow only about one centimeter. When a stalactite and a stalagmite finally meet, they join into a single stone pillar called a column.

Saudi Arabia has many caves, too. A large number lie beneath a dry area called the Summan Plateau, northeast of Riyadh. Some contain stalactites and stalagmites that formed long ago, when Arabia was much wetter. Scientists study their layers to learn how rainfall has changed.

Visitors should never touch these formations. The natural oil on human skin can stop them from growing.

versions.title: Hidden Halls of Stone: How Caves Grow
versions.text:
Venture into a limestone cave, and you will immediately notice the darkness and the cool, damp atmosphere. When a flashlight illuminates the ceiling, it reveals pointed formations of stone suspended like icicles, which geologists call stalactites, while similar formations, known as stalagmites, rise from the floor beneath them.

Most caves develop in limestone, a rock composed primarily of the mineral calcite. As rainwater passes through the atmosphere and the soil, it absorbs carbon dioxide, which converts it into a weak acid. This slightly acidic water trickles into microscopic cracks in the rock and gradually dissolves the surrounding limestone. Over hundreds of thousands of years, the cracks widen into tunnels, passages, and enormous chambers.

Even after a cave has formed, water continues seeping through its ceiling. Each droplet carries dissolved calcite, and when a droplet hangs from the ceiling, it releases some of its carbon dioxide, which causes it to deposit a thin ring of calcite. Ring by ring, a stalactite gradually lengthens downward, while droplets that fall to the floor deposit additional calcite that builds a stalagmite upward.

Many people mix up the two names, so here is a trick. A stalactite has a c, for ceiling, and it hangs from the top. A stalagmite has a g, for ground, and it grows up from the floor.

These formations develop remarkably slowly, frequently requiring a century to grow approximately one centimeter. When a stalactite and a stalagmite eventually merge, they create a single pillar called a column.

Saudi Arabia possesses numerous caves, many of them located beneath the dry As-Summan Plateau, northeast of Riyadh. Some of these caves contain stalactites and stalagmites that formed thousands of years ago, when the climate of Arabia was considerably wetter. Because their layers accumulate like the rings of a tree, scientists study them to understand how rainfall has changed over time.

Visitors should never touch these delicate formations, because the natural oils on human skin can prevent calcite from attaching to the surface, permanently stopping their growth.

This slightly acidic water seeps into tiny cracks in the bedrock and gradually dissolves the surrounding limestone, slowly widening those fractures into tunnels, passages, and enormous chambers over hundreds of thousands of years.

Even after a cave has formed, water continues seeping downward through its ceiling. Each droplet carries dissolved calcite, and when a droplet hangs from the ceiling, it releases some of its carbon dioxide into the cave air, which causes it to deposit a microscopic ring of calcite. Ring upon ring, a stalactite gradually lengthens downward, while droplets that splash onto the floor deposit additional calcite that builds a stalagmite upward.

Many people mix up the two names, so here is a trick. A stalactite has a c, for ceiling, and it hangs from the top. A stalagmite has a g, for ground, and it grows up from the floor.

These formations develop remarkably slowly, frequently requiring a century to grow approximately one centimeter. When a stalactite and a stalagmite eventually merge, they create a single continuous pillar called a column.

Saudi Arabia possesses numerous caves, many of them concentrated beneath the arid As-Summan Plateau, northeast of Riyadh. Some of these caves contain stalactites and stalagmites that formed thousands of years ago, when the climate of Arabia was considerably wetter. Because their layers accumulate like the rings of a tree, scientists analyze them to reconstruct how ancient rainfall patterns changed over time.

Visitors should never touch these delicate formations, because the natural oils on human skin can prevent calcite from adhering to the surface, permanently halting growth that required many centuries.

versions.title: Hidden Halls of Stone: How Caves Grow
versions.text:
Venture into a limestone cave, and you will immediately notice the profound darkness and the surprisingly cool, damp atmosphere that surrounds you. When a flashlight illuminates the ceiling, it reveals pointed formations of stone suspended like icicles, which geologists call stalactites, while similar formations, known as stalagmites, rise steadily from the floor beneath them. Exploring such a place feels like entering a hidden underground hall sculpted entirely by water.

Most caves originate in limestone, a sedimentary rock composed primarily of the mineral calcite, which formed from the shells and skeletons of ancient sea creatures. As rainwater percolates through the atmosphere and the overlying soil, it absorbs carbon dioxide, which transforms it into a weak carbonic acid. This slightly acidic water infiltrates microscopic cracks in the bedrock and gradually dissolves the surrounding limestone, progressively widening those fractures into tunnels, passages, and enormous chambers, a process that typically requires hundreds of thousands of years of uninterrupted chemical activity.

Even after a cave has formed, water continues seeping downward through its ceiling. Each droplet carries dissolved calcite, and when a droplet hangs from the ceiling, it releases some of its carbon dioxide into the cave air, which causes it to deposit a microscopic ring of calcite. Ring upon ring, a stalactite gradually lengthens downward, while droplets that splash onto the floor deposit additional calcite that constructs a stalagmite upward.

Because many people confuse the two terms, a convenient memory device can help: a stalactite contains the letter c, for ceiling, since it hangs from above, whereas a stalagmite contains the letter g, for ground, since it grows upward from the floor.

These formations develop remarkably slowly, frequently requiring an entire century to grow approximately one centimeter, which means that an impressive specimen may represent many thousands of years of patient accumulation. When a stalactite and a stalagmite eventually merge, they create a single continuous pillar called a column.

Saudi Arabia possesses numerous caves, many of them concentrated beneath the arid As-Summan Plateau, northeast of Riyadh. Some of these caves contain stalactites and stalagmites that formed thousands of years ago, when the climate of Arabia was considerably wetter than it is today. Because their layers accumulate like the rings of a tree, scientists carefully analyze them to reconstruct how ancient rainfall patterns changed over time, information that improves our understanding of the region's environmental history.

Visitors should never touch these delicate formations, because the natural oils on human skin can prevent calcite from adhering to the surface, permanently halting growth that required many centuries to accomplish.

questions.stem: What is this article mostly about?
options: How people long ago built their homes in caves
How caves form and how stone points grow in them
Why bats like to sleep in dark caves all day
How to find water to drink in the hot desert
questions.why: The article explains how rain makes caves and how drips make stalactites, stalagmites, and columns.

wrong.A: The article does not talk about homes in caves.
wrong.D: The article is about caves, not finding water.

questions.stem: In which kind of rock do most caves form?
options: Thick ice
Glass rock
Soft sand
Limestone
questions.why: The article says most caves form in a rock called limestone.

wrong.A: The stone points look like icicles, but caves do not form in ice.
wrong.B: Glass is not a rock in the article.
wrong.C: Sand is not named as the rock where caves form.

questions.stem: What is a stalactite?
options: A stone point that grows up from the floor
A post made when two points meet
A stone point that hangs down from the roof
A deep crack in the rock
questions.why: The article says the stone points that hang down like icicles are stalactites.

wrong.A: A point that grows up from the floor is a stalagmite.
wrong.B: A post made when two points meet is a column.
wrong.D: Cracks are where the rain sinks in, not stalactites.

questions.stem: In the article, a column is —
options: a stone post made when two points join
a drop of water from the roof
a gas that comes from the air
a dry land in Saudi Arabia
questions.why: The article says that when a stalactite and a stalagmite meet, they make a post called a column.

wrong.B: Drops of water drip from the roof, but they are not columns.
wrong.C: The gas makes rain a weak acid; it is not a column.
wrong.D: The dry land is called the Summan.

questions.stem: Why can rain slowly eat away limestone?
options: The rain is very hot when it falls.
The rain is full of sharp sand.
The rain falls very hard on it.
A gas makes the rain an acid.
questions.why: The article says rain picks up a gas that turns it into a weak acid, which eats the rock bit by bit.

wrong.A: The article does not say the rain is hot.
wrong.B: Sand is not given as the reason.
wrong.C: The article says the rock wears away bit by bit, not from hard rain.

questions.stem: How does the article explain how a stalactite grows?
options: It tells the steps in order, drip by drip.
It tells a story about a lost explorer.
It lists caves from biggest to smallest.
It compares caves with houses and shops.
questions.why: The article goes step by step: water drips, the drop lets the gas go, a ring of stone is left, and ring by ring the stalactite grows.

wrong.B: There is no story about an explorer.
wrong.C: Caves are not listed by size.
wrong.D: Caves are not compared to houses.

questions.stem: A visitor breaks off a stalactite. Why is this a big loss?
options: The cave will fall down that same day.
The stone will turn back into rain.
It took a very long time to grow.
The other stalactites will stop dripping.

wrong.B: Stone does not turn back into rain.
wrong.D: Other drips keep falling; the article does not say they stop.

questions.stem: The stone points in the Summan caves grew long ago. Why might few new ones grow there today?

There is less rain to drip in now.
People painted over all of the old ones.
The limestone has all turned into sand.

wrong.C: Nothing in the article says they were painted.
wrong.D: The article does not say the rock changed into sand.

MID.prompt: Explain how water both destroys rock and builds new stone inside a cave. Use evidence from the article.
checklist: I explained how water makes the cave.
I explained how water builds stalactites and stalagmites.
I used at least two details from the article.
MID.modelAnswer: Water destroys rock when rain mixes with gas in the air and slowly dissolves limestone, which widens cracks into tunnels and rooms over thousands of years. But water also builds new stone inside the cave: as drops seep through the ceiling, each one leaves behind a thin ring of mineral, so a stalactite slowly grows downward. Drops that fall to the floor leave mineral there too, so a stalagmite grows upward until the two sometimes join into a single column.

keyWords.definition: a common mineral that makes up limestone and cave formations
keyWords.example: Seashells are made largely of calcite.

keyWords.definition: to leave a layer of material behind
keyWords.example: The river will deposit fine mud on the fields after the flood.

keyWords.definition: the usual weather of a place over many years
keyWords.example: The climate of Jazan is hot and humid for much of the year.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the article?
options: Caves are formed mainly by earthquakes that crack the ground wide apart.
Water carves caves by dissolving limestone and builds formations from calcite.
Stalactites and stalagmites grow very quickly whenever it rains outside.
Scientists prefer studying caves in Saudi Arabia to studying caves elsewhere.
questions.why: The article explains how acidic water dissolves limestone into caves and how droplets deposit calcite to build stalactites, stalagmites, and columns.

wrong.A: The article credits acidic water, not earthquakes.
wrong.C: The article stresses that formations grow extremely slowly.
wrong.D: The article does not compare scientists' preferences.

questions.stem: According to the article, what turns rainwater into a weak acid?
options: Touching calcite on the cave floor
Mixing with salt from the sea
Freezing inside the cold cave
Absorbing carbon dioxide
questions.why: The article states that rainwater absorbs carbon dioxide, which converts it into a weak acid.

wrong.A: Calcite is what the water dissolves and later deposits; it does not make the acid.

questions.stem: According to the article, why do scientists study cave formations from the As-Summan Plateau?
options: To measure exactly how deep the caves go
To learn how the region's rainfall changed
To find out which animals live underground
To discover how to make new limestone
questions.why: The article says scientists study the layers to understand or reconstruct how rainfall has changed over time.

wrong.A: Cave depth is not discussed.
wrong.D: The article explains limestone's makeup, but that is not why scientists study the formations.

questions.stem: In the article, the word deposit most nearly means —
options: to wash away
to break apart
to leave behind
to soak up fully
questions.why: When a droplet deposits a ring of calcite, it leaves that mineral behind on the ceiling or floor.

wrong.A: Washing away is closer to what dissolving does.
wrong.B: The droplet builds, rather than breaks.
wrong.D: Soaking up is what the rain does with carbon dioxide.

questions.stem: What is the effect of touching a cave formation, according to the article?
options: It makes the formation grow much faster than before.
It turns the calcite on the surface into acid.
Skin oils can keep calcite from attaching.
It causes the whole column to split in two.
questions.why: The article explains that oils on human skin can prevent calcite from attaching, permanently stopping growth.

wrong.A: Touching harms growth; it does not speed it up.
wrong.B: Skin does not turn calcite into acid.
wrong.D: The article does not say columns split.

questions.stem: The article compares the layers of a formation to the rings of a tree. What does this comparison suggest?
options: The formations are actually made of wood.
Each layer records conditions from its time.
Trees once grew deep inside these caves.
Formations grow faster in summer than in winter.
questions.why: Tree rings mark the years of growth, so the comparison suggests that each layer holds a record of its own time, which is why scientists study it.

wrong.A: The formations are made of calcite.
wrong.C: The article does not mention trees in caves.
wrong.D: Seasonal growth rates are not discussed.

questions.stem: What can you infer about water in the As-Summan caves today compared with the past?
options: There is probably more water dripping into the caves now.
The water has always stayed exactly the same.
The water today is probably saltier than seawater.
There is probably less water than when the formations grew.
questions.why: The formations grew when Arabia's climate was wetter, and the plateau is now dry, so less water likely reaches the caves.

wrong.A: The article describes the plateau as dry or arid today.
wrong.B: The article says the climate changed.

questions.stem: How is the information about the formation of caves organized?
options: As a chain of causes and effects over time
As a list of the most famous caves in the world
As an argument for and against visiting caves
As a story told by one experienced cave explorer
questions.why: The article explains a chain: carbon dioxide makes acid, the acid dissolves limestone, cracks widen, and chambers form, then droplets deposit calcite.

wrong.B: Only the Saudi caves are named.
wrong.C: The article does not debate visiting caves.

HIGH.prompt: Cave formations have been called 'records written in stone.' Explain what this means, using evidence about how formations grow and what scientists learn from them.
checklist: I explained how formations grow layer by layer.
I explained what scientists learn from the layers.
I used precise evidence from the article.
HIGH.modelAnswer: Calling cave formations 'records written in stone' means that each ring of calcite left behind as water drips preserves a small piece of history, much like rings in a tree. Rainwater absorbs gas and becomes a weak acid that can dissolve limestone, and the dissolved calcite it carries is slowly deposited, layer by layer, to build stalactites and stalagmites. Because caves beneath Saudi Arabia's Summan Plateau contain formations that grew when the region's climate was much wetter, scientists can study these layers to learn exactly how rainfall has changed over time.
